title: Creating Pull Requests
key_takeaways: Pull requests are proposals to merge changes that create review opportunities and preserve decision context
GitHub Flow (branch → commit → push → PR → review → merge → delete) structures professional development
Upstream tracking (-u flag) simplifies future push operations for new branches
PR descriptions document 'why' behind changes - information not recoverable from code alone
Issue/PR linking with 'Closes #N' creates full traceability and auto-closes issues on merge
The 'Why' section in PR descriptions is most valuable long-term for understanding architectural decisions
Diff review catches unintended changes, formatting issues, and line ending problems before merge
PRs serve as remote backup for work-in-progress and enable multi-device workflows

catchbook_deliverable.description: Opened and merged PR #1 to add development workflow documentation to README
catchbook_deliverable.quality_assessment: Professional-grade PR with excellent description structure, proper issue linking, clean diff, and appropriate metadata

objectives_met: Understand what pull requests are and why they're essential for code review
Push feature branches to GitHub remote repository
Open a pull request through GitHub web interface
Write clear PR titles and descriptions using best practices
Link PRs to GitHub issues for traceability
Understand PR status checks and continuous integration basics
Apply PR workflow to CatchBook feature development
struggles: Initial uncertainty about merge commit message formatting (resolved through clarification)
Recognizing 'unknown unknowns' in PR description content (demonstrates healthy self-awareness rather than actual struggle)
misconceptions_noted: Minor: Thought -u flag applies when switching to any branch (clarified: only for new branches)
Minor: Unsure about status checks timing (clarified: they run on push, not during manual review)
